reviews.text:
Due to a job transfer this year, I've been forced to move between various animal hospitals in Tokyo, but I still haven't found a hospital I can trust as much as this one.

They saved our two Java sparrows.

One of them was particularly weak, but the doctor pinpointed the cause through blood tests, and thanks to the doctor's accurate diagnosis and medication, its life was saved.

I had been to several well-known hospitals in Osaka before, but this doctor was the one who finally identified the cause.

Even after moving to Tokyo, I've been to several well-known hospitals, but the treatment and examinations were all haphazard, and I haven't been able to find a hospital where I can truly entrust my pets with peace of mind.

It's truly a shame that I can't continue going there.

I honestly don't even want to give it one star.

I absolutely do not recommend it, and I cannot recommend it.

Last year, my 3-year-old budgie was killed by this vet. (I took the medical records from this vet to another bird specialist hospital, showed them the symptoms, condition, and videos, and after a detailed explanation, they said there was a strong possibility of medical malpractice.)
*I asked for the medical records after my bird died to confirm whether there had been any medical malpractice.

↓Here's what happened:

When I opened the sleeping cover, my bird was limping and lifting its leg.
So I took it to this vet, where I had been taking it before (it was energetic and had a good appetite).

It was diagnosed as a sprain and antibiotics were prescribed, but there was no improvement, so then steroids were prescribed.

I knew steroids were strong medications, so I asked if it was okay, but the vet said it was.

Although its leg improved, its other condition visibly worsened.

It started drinking an excessive amount of water, shaking its wings, its droppings became watery, and it began to curl up in a ball.

I consulted the vet about that too, but the vet ordered a blood test, thinking there might be something else wrong.
A blood test on a swollen, clearly unwell dog…
And it turned out to be kidney disease…
But the vet had been muttering things like, "He's only 3 years old, it's too early for it to get that bad?"
Besides, he was perfectly healthy except for his legs, so it was so sudden… huh?
I was filled with questions and my distrust grew.
I asked the vet many times if it really wasn't because of the steroids.
The vet said that since his kidneys were bad, he should drink plenty of water, and so on.
He passed away the next day.
My dog ​​suffered terribly, his breathing became labored, and he became confused, but he still desperately tried to eat and live. I called the vet again. No apology.
He insisted he was not at fault. That there was no medical malpractice.
He said the medication he prescribed was correct.

Going back to what I said above, I was so heartbroken and upset, and I felt so sorry for my child...he was only 3 years old...he was healthy, but the medicine the doctor prescribed weakened him, and he suffered terribly before passing away. I couldn't do anything but cry and apologize to my child...
So I went to the hospital in person and asked for his medical records.

The doctor said to me, "You knew that steroids were a strong medicine, yet you still gave it to him, didn't you?"

He even asked why I didn't bring him in sooner if I thought the symptoms were strange after giving him the medicine...
He even shifted the blame onto me.

Not only my other children, but my deceased child had been under their care for a long time, and we trusted them completely...

I never want to go back there again, and I will never forgive them.

Incidentally, I was told that the kidney values ​​were strongly influenced by the steroids. They said that he was already weakened, and with all the blood tests and other things piling up, he might have gone into shock...

Besides, steroids aren't meant to be taken for days on end, and they're usually only used in very critical situations. They said they wouldn't use them for something like a sprain. The steroids were quite strong, so it's not surprising that the kidney values ​​increased, and the reason the leg improved was because taking strong medication reduces pain... or so they said.

Later, when I looked up the medications I was prescribed, I found that some were drugs/supplements used for dogs and cats.

They weren't confirmed to be safe for birds.

They also ridiculed a well-known veterinarian at a certain bird hospital, calling him a heretic.

So, if you go, do so at your own risk... think carefully.

I just hope no one else becomes a victim.

I received excellent care when my conure was injured.

They examined him very carefully.

It's difficult to find a veterinary clinic that treats birds, so I was very grateful.

My female zebra finch's weight increased from 12g to 14g, and after several days there were no signs of her going into labor, so I took her to the vet to have her checked for eggs just in case.

The result was that she didn't have any eggs and it seemed she was just in heat. However, the moment the vet put her back in the cage after an ultrasound, I noticed she was limping as if favoring one leg, and I panicked and said, "Doctor! There's something wrong with her leg!"

The vet put his hand into the cage and checked her movements inside, saying, "That's not true," so I thought I might have been mistaken and went back to the waiting room.

However, I became worried in the waiting room and checked on her again, being careful not to let her escape. Despite being a wild bird, she didn't move at all when I touched her and kept her eyes closed.

Because her behavior was so strange, I told the receptionist and asked the vet to examine her again, but he just chased her around in the cage without doing anything. The bird was panicking, so I decided to take her home, thinking it would only cause her more stress.

Despite the ultrasound being performed to check for eggs, I was told there was no consultation fee and left without paying.

After taking her out of the cage at home, as you can see in the video, she couldn't open her eyes, couldn't put weight on her injured leg, and seemed to be having trouble breathing.
She had been fine all day, both at home and in the waiting room before the examination began. I only brought her in to check for eggs, and I never imagined she would be injured at the hospital.
I frantically called the hospital and tearfully confronted the doctor, who said, "I pulled her leg, but not that hard."
Then why didn't they charge me for the consultation?
Other reviews mentioned that they charged the consultation fee even when eggs were lost, so why didn't they charge me this time?
Why didn't they tell me that they had pulled her leg while she was in the examination room?
She was in so much pain that I took her back to the afternoon clinic to get pain medication.
At this time, the receptionist asked me a leading question: "Did the injury happen at home?"
This is the person who witnessed the entire sequence of events in the examination room during the morning consultation four hours earlier.

This is the person who, at the reception desk during the morning consultation, said, "The consultation fee is not required."

I believe this was likely at the doctor's instruction.

I clearly stated, "This injury occurred during the examination."

In the examination room, I instructed them not to touch the animal anymore, and they only observed it visually, prescribing pain medication.

At this time, the doctor made a strange excuse, saying, "I pulled its leg, but it was the other leg."

Even after giving the pain medication, the animal suffered for several days, so I think it must have been in considerable pain.

Furthermore, from that day forward, the animal stopped making any noise for six months.

I've researched this, and it seems that this can happen if the animal is severely shocked.

It may have been a momentary lapse in judgment, but the handling of the aftermath was extremely poor.

Perhaps they became careless because their job involves dealing with animals that cannot speak?

Have previous mistakes been covered up?

I had been a patient for many years, but I can no longer trust the doctor.

I hope that other people's beloved pets will be happy and not suffer.

The doctor and nurses were kind and thorough. I'm so glad I went to this clinic. They saved my budgie, who was in a dangerous condition due to undigested droppings and loss of appetite. In the evening, he suddenly couldn't perch and fell to the bottom of the cage, lying listlessly with his wings spread. His legs were shaking uncontrollably. Luckily, it was within their operating hours, so I called quickly and rushed him in for an emergency examination (it was his first visit). The phone service was also kind and thorough. I usually go to a different hospital, but that day was their day off. Even when I explained this (and that I would go to that hospital for future visits), they responded without showing any displeasure. The diagnosis was that he was dehydrated and in danger, so they immediately gave him an injection and force-fed him. He recovered remarkably quickly right before my eyes. They said, "It would be good to let him warm up a bit before you go home. Keeping him warm (28-30°C) is absolutely essential once you get home!" They left a heater for him for a while, and during that time they told me about treatment and diseases in birds in general. In particular, 2025 saw a prolonged period of extreme heat and humidity, followed by a sudden drop in temperature to near-winter levels. It was believed that the damage sustained during the summer, combined with the sudden temperature change, had caused a rapid deterioration in the digestive system's function. They said that it would only get worse if it wasn't kept warm. For the time being, I was told to keep it warm and at strict rest, and to administer antibiotics and gastrointestinal medication directly. However, at my usual hospital, we mix it with drinking water and let it drink naturally (free drinking), so I requested to continue using the same method, and they agreed without complaint. They said that blood tests and X-rays would be good, but since the dog is currently weakened, it would be dangerous to wait until it has recovered a bit more. The top priority was to restore its appetite with medication and ensure it receives proper nutrition. They didn't try to force any tests, which left a good impression on me, as it didn't seem like a hospital that would try to charge extra. As I was leaving, the nurse told me, "If it's an emergency, even without a prior appointment, we will see you if you come in during our clinic hours," which was a great relief. The next day was a holiday for the hospital. Although he was better than the day before, he was still not very energetic, so I took him to the original hospital after explaining that I had taken him to another hospital the day before. The vet said, "His condition isn't as bad as you described on the phone beforehand. I think the treatment and medication you prescribed the day before were correct, which is why he's recovering." He had recovered enough for an X-ray, and the vet confirmed, "As you suspected, he does have gastrointestinal problems." I'm so relieved, because if it weren't for the treatment the day before, he probably would have died! Within a week, he started eating normally again (mainly oats and small, hulled millet, which are easy to digest), and he regained his energy.

I visited this hospital after reading reviews and thinking it seemed like a good place.

I was considering having my bird's wings clipped, but when I asked about the stress it might cause, they didn't answer my questions and just kept pressuring me with "Are you going to clip them?! Or not?!"

Ultimately, I decided against it, thinking I'd rather go to a different hospital and have a proper doctor do it than have such a careless person do it. However, I was very dissatisfied because they exaggerated their claims about treating birds but didn't answer any of my questions.

On a separate note, the doctor's body odor when I entered the room was so strong it seemed like he hadn't showered in days.

I was shocked by the smell; it was hard to believe he was involved in animal medicine.

If you're treating your own family member, I think you should find a better hospital.

I don't want my precious family member to die from inadequate treatment, so I will never go there again.

My pet budgie had a leg problem, so I took it to the vet. They said it was a sprain and told me to give it steroids. I continued giving it to the vet, but its condition worsened. When I went back to the vet, they said it had kidney problems. They didn't explain the medication at all when they prescribed the steroids, and their service was terrible. When I researched and asked other vets, they all said they wouldn't give steroids for a sprain. My budgie had weak kidneys, so continuing to give it steroids triggered a deterioration in its condition, and it ultimately passed away. When I called to tell them about it, they pretended not to know or asked if they hadn't explained the medication, and they kept giving me different answers each time. They may have some knowledge, but they were not at all empathetic. I will never go there again.

Reservations are required online. I called several times but couldn't get through, so I couldn't explain my symptoms in advance and ask if they'd accept me. 🥲‎
I also had to pay for a taxi, which was a burden on my bird. …

My two parakeets are always taken care of here. 
I now need to make an appointment, but they are very thorough and I will continue to use their services.
Reservations are required. Please note that there are many small animals.
I visit this vet every few months for my Java sparrow's claw trimming and check-ups. They always examine him very carefully.

He looked at my cockatiel.
He's not a bird specialist, but I think he's one of the most knowledgeable about birds.
All of our budgies are cared for here. They receive attentive examinations and treatments that are tailored to their symptoms. Thank you so much as always.

My cockatiel was diagnosed with diabetes insipidus and prescribed Pitorecin to be administered directly into the bird's nose, along with an antibiotic. I've been taking it to the vet for almost a year, but it hasn't improved. The cockatiel dislikes having the medicine administered directly through its nose, so I took it to another vet in Minato, Sakai, who told me that you should never administer any medicine directly to a bird. I'm still going to this vet!
I've spent enough money to buy more than 10 cockatiels, but it hasn't been cured.
I intend to see it through to the end, but I'm worried about the future!

Please excuse the long message.

My irreplaceable and precious parakeet, which was flying around happily until 10 days ago, was killed by the head veterinarian. The circumstances were that although the symptoms weren't serious, I took it to the vet just in case. I followed the vet's instructions and refrained from letting it out of its cage. Afterward, its condition worsened, so I took it back to the evening clinic. I brought it home, but it hadn't improved the next day, so it eventually needed liquid food and had to be hospitalized.

I had taken it to the vet for various reasons over the years, but this was its first hospitalization.

Eventually, its condition only worsened.

Before the first time I took it to the vet, it was eating well, and I was worried about overeating, so I weighed it several times a day and carefully controlled the amount of food. As someone else has also posted, this head veterinarian would say unrealistic things, contradict what he had said before, and repeatedly state things I already knew, which was incredibly frustrating. I have experience hatching parakeets from eggs at home and have kept many in the past, so I believe I have a fair amount of knowledge. I believe the Nakatsu Group is a hospital that only cares about making money. Other hospitals (far away) have doctors who, even after just one visit, provide thorough phone consultations. However, I was told that a phone consultation with the hospital director would incur an additional charge. They even provided specific figures: 2,750 yen for 15 minutes and 5,500 yen for 30 minutes.

Since then, I've been too scared (not because of the money) to call, and have opted for getting brief answers through staff.

While it might be okay for first-time patients who are mentally strong, I absolutely do not recommend it to others. This is because the director is arrogant and scoffs at questions. Birds can't speak, so owners have to explain everything in detail, but the director doesn't listen to the end and starts talking forcefully, seemingly annoyed. One day, when I had to personally perform crop and stool tests due to a staff shortage, the director sighed heavily while holding the microscope slide. This happened more than once. I truly felt that he found it incredibly bothersome. Even when he messed up trimming my bird's claws and caused bleeding, he never apologized. I wished he would at least apologize to the bird that suffered, even if not to me. He also missed grabbing a small bird in the examination room several times, letting it escape. And unbelievably, he blamed the bird. He spoke to the bird as if it was being too energetic. In short, he lacks far too much as a person, even before considering his role as a veterinarian. Each member of the family runs their own practice, but they are all equally unfriendly. I truly felt that blood is thicker than water. Even if the wounds inflicted by the head veterinarian heal and I welcome a new bird into my home someday, I will never go back to this hospital. There's still so much more to write. If I wrote everything down, I could easily fill a thick notebook.

As an aside, this bird, killed by the head veterinarian, was cremated at a temple like a human, and the head priest performed a respectful service, including the first seven days of mourning. After it was over, I received kind words from the head priest, which was a great comfort. It's wrong to even compare them, but I couldn't help but wonder how such a difference could exist between two people. Also, as mentioned in the text, even though I had only taken my pet to this veterinarian once, he kindly listened to my concerns over the phone. When I tearfully reported what had happened to him, he offered his condolences and even gave me comforting advice that helped me to calm down. Of course, the director of the hospital where my pet died didn't offer any condolences at all; instead, he indirectly told me to come and pick up my pet as soon as possible because it would deteriorate if left there, perhaps because the hospital was closed the next day. If you love your pet, who is a member of your family, and want them to live as long as possible, I think it would be wise not to take them to this hospital.
